# Disagreement Log — Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 63

**Date:** 2026-03-17
**Agents:** EMET (literal) | LOGOS (formal) | PNEUMA (dynamic)
**Total Disagreements:** 9

---

## Disagreement 1 — 63:1 "thinking over the commandments" vs. "meditating on"

- **EMET:** "thinking over the commandments how they were beautiful"
- **LOGOS:** "meditating on the commandments — how they were beautiful"
- **PNEUMA:** "turning the commandments over in my mind"
- **Greek:** *dialogizomenos tas entolas* — deliberating on/going through the commandments
- **Ruling:** SOPHIA uses "meditating on the commandments" (LOGOS). *Dialogizomenos* = thinking through deliberately; "meditating on" captures the focused reflection.

---

## Disagreement 2 — 63:1 "glad" — description of commandments

- **EMET:** "how they were beautiful and powerful and glad"
- **LOGOS:** "how they were beautiful and powerful and glad"
- **PNEUMA:** "how beautiful, powerful, joyful, and glorious they were"
- **Greek:** *hilara kai endoxa* — cheerful/merry and glorious
- **Ruling:** SOPHIA uses "beautiful and powerful and glad and glorious." EMET and LOGOS agree; "glad" is an unusual description for commandments but reflects the Greek *hilaros*.

---

## Disagreement 3 — 63:2 "double-minded about the commandments" vs. "doubting"

- **EMET:** "why are you double-minded about the commandments"
- **LOGOS:** "why are you double-minded about the commandments"
- **PNEUMA:** "Why are you still doubting the commandments"
- **Note:** EMET and LOGOS agree.
- **Ruling:** SOPHIA uses "why are you double-minded about the commandments." *Dipsychain* = to be double-minded; "double-minded" preserves the technical vocabulary of the Mandates.

---

## Disagreement 4 — 63:3 "this commandment is especially welcome to me" vs. "especially pleases me"

- **EMET:** "this commandment is especially welcome to me"
- **LOGOS:** "this commandment especially pleases me"
- **PNEUMA:** "this commandment especially resonates with me"
- **Greek:** *hē entolē hautē...areskei moi* — this commandment pleases me
- **Ruling:** SOPHIA uses "this commandment especially pleases me" (LOGOS). *Areskei* = pleases/is pleasing; "resonates" (PNEUMA) is too contemporary.

---

## Disagreement 5 — 63:3 "kept myself pure from women" vs. "kept myself chaste"

- **EMET:** "kept myself pure from women, from every kind of adultery and impurity"
- **LOGOS:** "kept myself chaste — from women and from every kind of adultery and impurity"
- **PNEUMA:** "kept myself sexually pure — free from women, from adultery, from every form of sexual impurity"
- **Greek:** *emeautou etērēsa apo gynaikos...moicheias...akatharsia* — I have kept myself from women, from adultery, from impurity
- **Ruling:** SOPHIA uses "kept myself chaste — from women and from every kind of adultery and impurity" (LOGOS). "Chaste" names the virtue that the list exemplifies; PNEUMA adds "sexually" three times, over-specifying.

---

## Disagreement 6 — 63:3 "bear testimony to it" vs. "bear witness to it"

- **EMET:** "the Spirit which dwells in it may bear testimony to it"
- **LOGOS:** "the Spirit that dwells in it may bear witness to it"
- **PNEUMA:** "the Spirit living in it can bear testimony to it"
- **Greek:** *martyrēsē autē* — may bear witness/testimony to it
- **Ruling:** SOPHIA uses "the Spirit that dwells in it may bear witness to it" (LOGOS). "Bear witness" is slightly more natural in English; "testimony" (EMET/PNEUMA) is also accurate.

---

## Disagreement 7 — 63:3 "your flesh may be justified" — all agree

- **EMET:** "your flesh may be justified"
- **LOGOS:** "your flesh may be justified"
- **PNEUMA:** "your body may be justified"
- **Greek:** *dikaiōthēsetai hē sarx* — the flesh will be justified
- **Ruling:** SOPHIA uses "your flesh may be justified." *Sarx* = flesh (technical term); PNEUMA's "body" loses the *sarx*-theology precision.

---

## Disagreement 8 — 63:4 "any thought enter into your heart" vs. "any thought should enter your heart"

- **EMET:** "lest any thought enter into your heart"
- **LOGOS:** "lest any thought should enter your heart"
- **PNEUMA:** "don't let any thought get into your mind"
- **Greek:** *mēpote ennoias tis eiselthē* — lest any thought enter
- **Ruling:** SOPHIA uses "lest any thought enter your heart" (EMET simplified). The heart (*kardia*) is the locus of thought in Hermas; PNEUMA's "mind" is an acceptable gloss but loses the *kardia* emphasis.

---

## Disagreement 9 — 63:4 "works death" vs. "brings death"

- **EMET:** "it works death"
- **LOGOS:** "it brings death"
- **PNEUMA:** "it brings death"
- **Greek:** *thanaton ergazetai* — works/produces death
- **Ruling:** SOPHIA uses "it brings death" (LOGOS/PNEUMA). "Works death" (EMET) is a legitimate Pauline idiom (cf. 2 Cor 7:10) but "brings death" is clearer in English.

---

*End of disagreement log for Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 63.*
